unit.title: Maintain a safe, clean and efficient work environment

summary: This unit teaches you to keep a salon safe, clean and well run: spot hazards and judge risks, control infection, store and handle chemicals, use electrical equipment, prevent and respond to fire, avoid slips, trips and strain, give first aid and report accidents, protect your own health, and work efficiently by saving electricity, water and products and by keeping a clean, tidy routine.

blocks.p: Every unit in your course rests on this one. A salon has water, electricity, heat, sharp tools, chemicals and close contact with people. Used carelessly they cause scalds, shocks, burns, cuts, fires, infections and strained backs. Used well they cause none of these, and the salon looks clean and professional, runs on time and costs less to run.
This unit is for COSMETOLOGY LEVEL 2 trainees. It applies to hair, nail, skin and make-up services alike. You will use it from your first day in the training salon.

blocks.note: How you are assessed: theory papers (multiple-choice questions, short answers and essays) and practical tasks in the Centre's training salon. In the practical tasks you carry out a hazard check and risk assessment of the salon and make a safety poster, then clean, disinfect and reset the salon, sort waste and check the chemical store. The assessor watches whether you use gloves, mix disinfectant correctly, handle blades safely and fill in the cleaning log, not only whether the salon looks clean.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Word
Meaning
Example
rows: Hazard
Anything that could cause harm.
Water on the floor; a split cable; a bleach bottle with no label.
Risk
How likely it is that the hazard will cause harm, and how bad the harm could be.
A wet floor by the busy basin is a high risk; the same puddle in a locked store room is a low one.
Control
What you do to remove or reduce the risk.
Wipe the floor, put out a wet floor sign.
Near miss
An event that could have caused injury or damage but did not.
A stylist trips on a cable but does not fall.
Accident
An event that does cause injury or damage.
A client slips and sprains an ankle.

flow: Look around and find the hazards
Decide who could be harmed and how
Judge how likely and how serious the harm would be
Decide the controls and who will do them
Record what you found and did
Review it regularly and after any accident or change

head: Hazard
Who could be harmed
Likelihood and seriousness
Control
rows: Trailing cable across a walkway
Everyone, clients most
Likely; could cause a fall and injury
Move the equipment; tuck cables away; unplug when not used
Open bottle of relaxer on a station
Stylists, clients, children
Possible; serious burns
Close it and return it to the locked store; gloves when in use
Hot flat iron left on a chair
Anyone sitting or touching it
Likely; serious burns
Use a heat-proof stand; unplug after use
Heavy box in the walkway
Everyone
Likely; trips and back strain
Store on a low shelf; lift correctly

ul: **Rank** the risks: deal first with what is most likely and most serious. A hazard that could burn or electrocute someone comes before an untidy shelf.
If you can fix a small hazard safely, fix it: wipe a spill, put a bag away. If you cannot, **warn others** (a sign, a cone, a barrier), **do not leave it**, and **report it to the supervisor**.
Report hazards even if nobody has been hurt, so they are fixed **before** an accident happens. Report near misses too: they are warnings.
Do not try repairs you are not trained or allowed to do.

blocks.note: The best controls remove the hazard completely (take the cable away). Next best: reduce it (a cable cover). Last: protect people from it (gloves, a sign). Signs and gloves do not make a hazard disappear.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Sign
Meaning
Example
rows: Red circle with a bar
Prohibition: you must not
No smoking; do not use water on electrical fires
Blue circle
Mandatory: you must
Wear gloves; wear eye protection
Yellow triangle
Warning: take care
Wet floor; electricity; flammable
Green rectangle
Safe condition: where to go or find help
Fire exit; first aid
Red rectangle
Fire equipment
Fire extinguisher; alarm call point

blocks.note: Put out a **wet floor sign** while a mopped or spilled floor is wet, and take it away when the floor is dry. A sign left out all day is ignored.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Pathogens (germs that cause disease) pass from person to person on hands, tools, towels, basins and surfaces. Bacteria cause infections such as impetigo; viruses cause colds, flu, warts and cold sores; fungi cause ringworm and athlete's foot; head lice are parasites.

flow: Wet your hands and wrists
Lather with soap
Rub palms, backs of hands, between the fingers, thumbs and under the nails for about 20 seconds
Rinse well
Dry with a clean towel or paper towel
Turn off the tap with the paper towel

ul: Wash before and after every client, after the toilet, before eating, after handling waste or chemicals, and after blowing your nose.
Alcohol hand sanitiser is useful when your hands are not visibly dirty, but it does not replace washing.
Cover cuts on your hands with a waterproof plaster. Do not work on clients if you have an infection that could spread.

head: Level
What it does
Used for
rows: Cleaning
Removes hair, dirt, oil and product with detergent and water. Comes first, always.
Every tool and surface
Disinfecting
Kills most germs, if the disinfectant is mixed as the label says and the tool stays covered for the contact time.
Combs, brushes, clips, clippers' blades, basins, chairs, work surfaces
Sterilising
Kills all germs, including spores. An **autoclave** uses steam under pressure.
Metal tools that may touch blood or broken skin, if the salon has the equipment

flow: Put on gloves
Remove hair and debris
Wash in warm water with detergent; scrub; rinse
Immerse fully in disinfectant mixed as the label says, for the full contact time
Rinse if the label says so; dry with a clean towel
Store in a clean, closed container or UV cabinet

ul: **Why clean first?** Hair and dirt stop the disinfectant reaching the surface of the tool.
A **UV cabinet** only keeps clean, disinfected tools clean while stored. It does **not** disinfect dirty ones.
Mix disinfectant exactly as the label says. Too weak will not work; too strong can harm skin and tools. Change the solution as often as the maker says, and when it looks dirty.
**Contact time** is how long a tool must stay wet with disinfectant. Use the time on the label.

blocks.p: A label that says 1 part disinfectant to 9 parts water means 10 parts in all. For 1 litre (1000 ml) of solution: 1000 ÷ 10 = 100 ml of disinfectant, and 900 ml of water. For 500 ml: 50 ml of disinfectant and 450 ml of water. Always use a measuring jug, not guesswork, and **add the disinfectant to the water** unless the label says otherwise.

head: Ratio on the label
Total parts
Disinfectant needed for 1 litre
rows: 100 ml
50 ml
200 ml

ul: **Single-use** items (neck strips, gloves, cotton, emery boards, wooden sticks, razor blades) are used once and thrown away.

**Razors and blades** are never shared or reused: they can carry blood-borne viruses such as hepatitis B, hepatitis C and HIV. Used blades go in a **sharps box**: puncture-proof, with a lid and a fill line, never pushed down with your fingers, and not overfilled.
If a client is nicked: put on gloves, press a clean pad of gauze or cotton on the cut until it stops, offer a plaster, clean and then disinfect or sterilise the tool, bag soiled waste, and record it.
Fresh towel and gown for every client; used ones go straight into a closed laundry bin.
Wash hot (as hot as the fabric allows) with detergent and dry completely: damp towels grow bacteria and mildew.
Wipe chairs, basins, trolleys and counters with disinfectant after each client.

blocks.note: Never work on a client with a contagious condition such as head lice, ringworm or impetigo. Explain kindly and privately and suggest she sees a doctor or pharmacist. Afterwards bag the towels for a hot wash and clean and disinfect everything she touched.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Relaxers, colours, peroxide, perm solutions, acetone, disinfectants and cleaners are hazardous chemicals.
Store in a **cool, dry, well-ventilated, locked place**, out of direct sunlight and away from heaters, children and clients.
Keep every chemical in its **own labelled container**. Never pour one into a drink bottle or unlabelled bottle: someone could drink or mix it.
Heavy containers on low shelves; lids on tightly; the oldest stock at the front (first in, first out).
Do not store chemicals above the basins or where they could fall. Keep different chemicals apart, and keep peroxide and strong oxidisers away from other products.
Keep the safety data sheets (SDS) where staff can find them.

blocks.note: Jamaica's heat can make chemicals spoil or build up pressure. A shelf in a hot, sunny room is not 'cool and dry'.
blocks.label: Jamaica

head: Do
Why
rows: Read the label and follow the maker's instructions
Strength, timing and mixing are set for safety.
Read the safety data sheet for hazards, PPE and first aid
It gives the full facts.
Wear PPE: gloves; apron; eye protection if there is a splash risk
Prevents burns and dermatitis.
Work in a ventilated area
Fumes can harm breathing.
Mix only what you need
Mixed chemicals go off and cannot be stored.
Never mix different products or brands
They can react. Bleach and ammonia-based cleaners give off a poisonous gas.
Wipe spills at once; close lids after use
Prevents slips, burns and fumes.

blocks.note: **PPE** means personal protective equipment: gloves, aprons, eye protection and masks. It protects you only if you wear it, keep it clean and replace it when damaged. Wash your hands after taking gloves off.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Where
What to do first
rows: In the eye

Rinse at once with plenty of clean, cool running water for at least 15 minutes, holding the eye open and tilting the head so water runs away from the other eye. Do not rub. Get medical help and take the label.
On the skin
Rinse with plenty of running water; remove contaminated clothing; get medical help if burned or sore.
Breathed in
Move to fresh air.
Swallowed
Do not make the person vomit. Get medical help at once; take the label.

flow: Warn people and keep them away
Put out a sign
Read the label and SDS
Ventilate
Put on gloves, apron and eye protection
Soak up from the outside inwards with paper towels or the spill kit
Bag the waste and dispose of it as the SDS says
Wash the area with detergent and water and dry it
Wash your hands
Report and record

head: Waste
Where it goes
rows: Cut hair, paper, cotton
Swept up after each client into a covered bin
Used razor blades and sharp items
A sharps box
Soiled towels and gowns
A closed laundry bin
Empty chemical containers and leftover mixtures
As the maker's instructions and the local rules say; do not pour large amounts down the drain
Aerosol cans
Never pierced or burned; empty cans as the local rules say
Pads soaked in flammable products
A lined metal bin with a lid, emptied daily

blocks.p: Never burn salon waste or pour chemicals into a gully or drain that runs to the road: it can poison people and animals and harm the environment.
Wet work and products can cause **dermatitis**: red, dry, itchy, cracked skin on your hands. Wear gloves for wet work and chemicals, dry your hands well, use hand cream, and report sore skin early.
Jamaica's power supply is 110 V (220 V for some heavy equipment) at **50 Hz**. Water and electricity together cause shocks, so basins, steamers and wet floors need special care.

head: Before use
During use
After use
rows: Check the plug is not cracked
Check the cable has no splits or bare wires
Check the casing is not damaged
Check that it is made for the supply
Dry hands only
Keep away from water and basins
One tool per socket; do not overload with adaptors
Keep cables tidy and out of walkways
Rest hot tools on a heat-proof stand
Switch off
Unplug by the plug, not the cable
Let it cool before cleaning or storing
Do not wrap the cable tightly round a hot tool

ul: Do not overload a socket: too many tools on one socket or extension can overheat the wiring and start a fire.
Do not use a faulty tool. **Switch off, unplug, label 'Do not use' and report it.** Only a **qualified person** repairs electrical equipment.
After a power cut or a storm, check equipment before reuse: a burning smell or a spark means unplug it at once.
Before cleaning a dryer or iron: switch off, unplug and let it cool.
If someone is being shocked, do not touch them: switch off at the socket or main switch, or knock them away with a dry wooden object, then call for help.

blocks.p: A fire needs three things: **heat, fuel and oxygen**. Take any one away and the fire goes out. Salons hold plenty of fuel: aerosols, alcohol-based products, paper, towels, chemicals, hair and plastic.

head: Prevent fires by
Why
rows: Switching off and unplugging tools after use
Removes the heat.
Not overloading sockets; reporting faulty equipment
Overheated wiring is a common cause.
Keeping aerosols and alcohol products away from heat and flames; never piercing cans
They can burn or burst.
Storing towels, paper and chemicals away from heaters and hot tools
Keeps fuel away from heat.
No smoking, candles or naked flames
Removes the spark.
Emptying rubbish daily
Removes fuel.
Keeping exits clear and extinguishers checked
So people can get out and the fire can be fought.

head: Extinguisher
Use on
Never on
rows: Water (usually red label)
Paper, wood, cloth
Electrical equipment, flammable liquids
Carbon dioxide (CO2, usually black label)
Electrical fires; flammable liquids
Nothing special in a salon; use in a ventilated space
Dry powder
Mixed fires: wood, liquids, electrical
Enclosed rooms (the powder is hard to breathe)
Fire blanket
Small fires in a pan or on a person; smothering a flammable liquid
Large fires

blocks.note: Colour codes vary; read the label on the extinguisher and know your salon's. Never use water on an electrical fire or a flammable liquid.
blocks.label: Safety

flow: Raise the alarm
Call the fire service
Stop work and switch off equipment if it is safe
Guide clients out by the nearest exit to the meeting point, leaving belongings
Only trained staff fight a small fire, with a safe way out behind them
Check everyone is out and never go back in

blocks.note: In Jamaica the emergency numbers are 110 for fire and ambulance and 119 for the police. Know your salon's meeting point and the position of the exits. Fire exits must always be clear and unlocked while the salon is open.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: Slips, trips, lifting and your own health

head: Cause
Control
rows: Water, hair or product on the floor
Wipe or sweep up at once; wet floor sign until dry.
Trailing cables
Tuck them away; use sockets near the stations; cable covers.
Bags, boxes and stock in walkways
Store them in the store room or on shelves.
Poor lighting
Keep lights working; report failures.
Worn or loose floor covering, cracked tiles
Report; mark the area; repair.
Unsuitable shoes
Closed, flat, non-slip shoes.

flow: Look at it: is it too heavy? Get help or use a trolley
Stand close, feet apart, one foot slightly forward
Bend your knees and keep your back straight
Grip firmly and hold the load close to your body
Lift by straightening your legs, not your back
Do not twist; move your feet to turn
Put it down the same way

ul: Adjust the client's chair to a height where you do not stoop or reach up; raise it for cutting, lower it for blow-drying tall clients.
Stand with your weight on both feet; move your feet instead of twisting; keep your elbows close.
Change position often; stretch your neck, shoulders and back between clients.
Take your breaks, eat and drink water. Tiredness causes mistakes with heat and chemicals.
A clean uniform each day; closed, flat shoes to protect the feet from spills, dropped tools and slips.
Long hair tied back; nails short and clean; minimal jewellery that could scratch clients or catch in equipment.
Shower, use deodorant, keep your breath fresh: you work very close to people.
Carry scissors with the points **down**, and pass them handle first.
Stay at home and tell your supervisor if you have an infection that could spread.

blocks.note: Do not walk about the salon with scissors or a razor in your pocket. Put sharp tools away in a holder or a closed case.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: A **first aider** is a person trained to give first aid at work. Know who they are and where the **first aid box** is: marked, easy to reach, stocked, and checked regularly. Never keep it locked in a car or a store room behind chemicals.
A box usually holds plasters, sterile dressings, bandages, gloves, antiseptic wipes, scissors, tape and an eye wash. Replace what is used.

head: Injury
First aid
rows: Minor cut
Gloves on; press a clean pad until bleeding stops; clean; dressing or plaster.
Burn or scald
Cool under cool running water for about 20 minutes; cover loosely; no butter, creams or ice; do not burst blisters.
Chemical in the eye
Rinse with plenty of clean running water; medical help.
Electric shock
Switch off the power first; do not touch the person until it is off; call for help.
Fainting
Lay her flat with the legs raised; fresh air; do not give food or drink until she recovers.
Serious injury
Call an ambulance (110); keep the person calm and still.

flow: Make the area safe
Call the first aider (and an ambulance if serious)
Give first aid with gloves if there is blood
Tell the supervisor
Write it in the accident book: date, time, place, name, what happened, injury, first aid given, witnesses
Restock the first aid box
Find the cause and prevent it happening again

sections.title: Working efficiently: cleaning, saving and stock

head: When
What is done
rows: At opening
Check the salon is clean and dry; wipe stations and mirrors
Check equipment and cables; fresh towels and gowns out
Restock stations; check the first aid box
After each client
Sweep hair into the covered bin
Clean and disinfect combs, brushes, clips
Wipe the chair, armrests and counter; clear and wipe the basin
Used towels to the laundry bin; wash hands
During the day
Clean as you go: wipe spills at once
Empty bins when full; check the toilet and staff area
At closing
Clean and disinfect all tools; wash and disinfect basins, chairs and surfaces
Sweep and mop with a wet floor sign out
Empty bins; wash laundry hot and dry it fully
Close products and put them away; switch off and unplug equipment; lock up

blocks.p: **Clean as you go** means tidying and cleaning during and after each task, so work never piles up. It is **housekeeping**: the daily work of keeping the salon clean, tidy and in order. Keep a cleaning log with the time, the job and your name.

ul: Use one product at a time and the strength the label gives. **Never mix** cleaning chemicals.
Wear gloves for cleaning chemicals; ventilate.
Use separate cloths for the toilet and for work surfaces; wash cloths daily; change mop water.

head: Resource
How to save it
rows: Electricity
Switch off and unplug tools, dryers and steamers when not in use
Switch off lights and fans in empty rooms
Keep doors closed when air conditioning is on
Wash full loads of towels
Water
Turn taps off between rinses
Report dripping taps and leaks at once: they waste water and money
Do not run the basin while you talk
Products
Use the right amount for the length and thickness of the hair
Close lids; store as the maker says so products do not spoil
Use the oldest stock first and check expiry dates

blocks.p: Saving matters because water and electricity cost a great deal in Jamaica, and waste raises the salon's costs and lowers what it can pay. It also protects the environment.

ul: **First in, first out (FIFO)**: new stock goes behind old, so the oldest is used first and nothing goes out of date.
Give each tool and product its own place, so things are quick to find and nothing is left out or lost.
Report low, damaged, leaking or out-of-date stock to your supervisor.

blocks.p: Cockroaches, ants, rats and flies carry germs and spoil products. Control them by keeping the salon clean, closing bins, not leaving food or drink out overnight, sealing gaps, and reporting any sign of pests to your supervisor, who arranges treatment. Do not spray insecticide near clients, towels or products.

ul: I can tell a hazard from a risk and say what a near miss is.
I can carry out a simple risk assessment and report a hazard.
I can wash my hands correctly and explain when to do it.
I can clean, disinfect, sterilise and store tools, and explain why cleaning comes first.
I can mix disinfectant by ratio and use the contact time.
I can handle sharps, blood and laundry safely.
I can store, label, use and dispose of chemicals, and deal with a spill or splash.
I can use electrical equipment safely and report faults.
I can name the three parts of the fire triangle, choose the right extinguisher and lead an evacuation.
I can prevent slips and trips, lift safely and keep good posture.
I can give basic first aid and complete the accident book.
I can protect my skin and keep a professional appearance.
I can follow a daily cleaning routine, save resources and rotate stock.

blocks.note: In essays, give the reason: 'I clean tools before disinfecting, because hair and dirt stop the disinfectant reaching the surface.'
blocks.label: Tip

terms: How likely a hazard is to cause harm, and how serious.
An event that could have caused injury but did not.
Finding hazards, judging risks and deciding controls.
A germ that can cause disease.
How long a tool must stay wet with disinfectant.
A machine that sterilises with steam under pressure.
A cabinet for storing clean, disinfected tools; it does not disinfect.
A puncture-proof container for used blades.

Personal protective equipment: gloves, aprons, eye protection.

c1.title: A late Friday in Montego Bay
c1.text: It is 4 p.m. on a busy Friday at a salon in Montego Bay. Trainee Jovan notices that water has dripped from the back-wash basin onto the tiles beside the first station. A hood dryer is plugged into an extension strip with four other tools, and the strip lies across the floor between two stations. Nearby, a client has just sat down.

c2.title: Mixing disinfectant in Mandeville
c2.text: At the end of the day at a training salon in Mandeville, trainee Alecia must prepare 2 litres of disinfectant for the combs and brushes. The label says to mix 1 part disinfectant with 19 parts water and keep tools in it for 10 minutes. She also has a stainless steel razor handle with a used blade, and a bottle of bleach and a bottle of an ammonia-based floor cleaner left on the trolley.

c3.title: A relaxer splash in Portmore
c3.text: While rinsing a relaxer at a salon in Portmore, stylist Natalee gets a splash of the cream into her left eye. The salon's first aid box is in the owner's car, which has gone out. The salon is crowded and the owner's office, where the safety data sheets are kept, is locked.

c4.title: A burning smell in Spanish Town
c4.text: At a salon in Spanish Town, the power goes off during a thunderstorm and comes back on a few minutes later. A hood dryer now smells of burning, and there is a thin wisp of smoke from its back. A client is sitting under it. Next to the dryer there is a pile of used towels, and a can of hairspray stands on top of it.

c5.title: Stock and savings in Savanna-la-Mar
c5.text: A small salon in Savanna-la-Mar has high electricity and water bills. The owner finds new boxes of shampoo stacked in front of old ones, two dripping basin taps, and dryers left switched on all day. Trainee Roxanne is asked to help fix this and to deal with a delivery of eight heavy 5-litre bottles of conditioner.

questions.q: What should Jovan do first about the water on the floor beside the first station?
o: Mop it later, when the rush has finished
Wipe it up now and put a wet floor sign out
Tell the client to step around it carefully
Put a towel over it so that it is not seen
questions.why: A wet floor near stations is a likely slip hazard. Deal with it at once: wipe it dry, and use a wet floor sign until it is dry. Covering it hides it and does not make it safe.

questions.q: What is the main danger of the extension strip with five tools plugged into it?
o: Overloading it can overheat the wiring and cause a fire
It will make the dryers run noticeably more slowly
The tools will use up more electricity on the bill
It will make the cables too short to reach the chairs
questions.why: Too many tools on one socket draw more current than the wiring should carry, so it overheats. Plug each high-power tool into its own socket and do not overload extension strips.

questions.q: Why is the strip lying across the floor between the stations also a problem?
o: It is a trip hazard and could drag tools off the station
It stops the cleaner from sweeping the hair away properly
It makes the stylists stand too close to the clients
It will wear out the carpet or tiles under it
questions.why: A cable in a walkway is a trip hazard: someone can fall, or drag a hot tool off the station. Move the equipment, tuck cables away, and keep walkways clear.

questions.q: Jovan tells the supervisor about the wet floor and the cables, although nobody has been hurt. Why is this right?
o: So that the salon can find out who to blame
So that clients can be told to leave the salon
So that they can be fixed before an accident happens
So that the supervisor can fill in the accident book
questions.why: Reporting hazards before anyone is hurt lets the salon fix them in time. Reporting is not about blame, and nothing goes in the accident book until an accident has happened.

questions.q: Alecia must fill a 2-litre jug with the 1 to 19 mixture. How much water goes in with the disinfectant?
questions.why: 1 part to 19 parts makes 20 parts in all. 2 litres is 2 000 ml, so 1 part is 100 ml of disinfectant, leaving 1 900 ml of water. Measure both with a jug.

questions.q: How should the combs and brushes be prepared before they go into the disinfectant?
o: Rinsed under the tap and left to dry on the trolley
Soaked with the disinfectant first, then brushed clean
Cleaned of hair and washed in warm, soapy water, then rinsed
Wiped with a damp cloth and placed straight into the solution
questions.why: Hair, dirt and product stop the disinfectant reaching the surface, so tools are cleaned first: hair removed, washed with detergent, rinsed. Only then are they immersed for the full contact time.

questions.q: The sharps box is full to its fill line when Alecia has one more blade. What is the right action?
o: Close and seal it, and start a new box for the blade
Push the blade down with a pen so it fits in the box
Wrap the blade in tissue and drop it in the bin
Leave the blade on the shelf until the box is emptied
questions.why: A sharps box is never overfilled or pushed down: blades can stab the next hand. At the fill line, close and seal it for safe disposal and start a new box.

questions.q: Alecia wants to use the bleach and the ammonia-based floor cleaner together to clean the basin 'extra well'. What should she be told?
o: Fine, as long as the windows are closed to keep the smell in
Fine, if she uses less of each than the labels say
Never mix them: they can react and give off a poisonous gas
Only mix them when the floor is wet so that they dilute
questions.why: Different cleaning chemicals must never be mixed. Bleach and ammonia-based cleaners react and release a toxic gas. Use one product at a time, as the label says, with ventilation and gloves.

questions.q: What is the first thing Natalee should do for her eye?
o: Rub it hard with a dry towel to get the cream out
Rinse it with plenty of clean, cool running water
Put a few drops of conditioner in it to soothe it
Keep the eye shut until she has finished the client
questions.why: Speed matters with a chemical in the eye. Rinse at once with plenty of clean running water for at least 15 minutes, holding the eye open and keeping the water running away from the other eye, then get medical help.

questions.q: What should happen about the client under the relaxer while Natalee rinses her eye?
o: A colleague takes over and rinses the client at once
The client stays as she is, because rinsing could wait
Natalee rinses her own eye and then returns to her client
The client must carry on rinsing her own hair alone
questions.why: Relaxer left on the client's scalp can burn it, so another trained person must take over and rinse at once. Natalee's eye injury comes first, and good teamwork keeps the client safe.

questions.q: What should the salon change after this, to be better prepared?
o: Keep the safety data sheets locked in the owner's office
Keep the first aid box in the car so it is not used up
Keep the first aid box and SDS where staff can reach them
Stop using relaxers unless the owner is in the salon
questions.why: First aid supplies and safety data sheets must be marked and easy to reach when needed, not locked away or taken out. Record the accident and review how it happened.

questions.q: What should the stylist do first about the dryer that smells of burning?
o: Turn the heat to low so that the smell goes away
Spray a little water on the back to cool it down
Leave it running to see if the smell stops by itself
Switch it off, unplug it, and help the client out
questions.why: A burning smell and smoke mean a serious electrical fault. Switch off at the socket and unplug it, look after the client, then label it 'Do not use' and report it. Never use water on live electrical equipment.

questions.q: A small flame starts at the back of the dryer. Which extinguisher is suitable for it?
o: A water extinguisher, sprayed from the front
A CO2 extinguisher, used by a trained person
A bucket of water from the nearest basin
A wet towel thrown over the whole dryer
questions.why: Water conducts electricity and can cause shock. A CO2 (or dry powder) extinguisher is suitable for electrical fires, and only trained staff should use it, with a safe way out. Switch off at the socket first if it is safe.

questions.q: Why is the hairspray can standing on a pile of towels beside the dryer a hazard?
o: Aerosols can burst or burn near heat, and towels are fuel
The towels will take up the spray and so need washing
The hairspray will go out of date in the heat of the dryer
The can will leave a ring on the towels
questions.why: Aerosols can burst or catch fire when heated, and towels are fuel. Heat, fuel and oxygen together make a fire. Keep aerosols away from heat and flames and store towels away from heaters and hot tools.

questions.q: After the incident, the stylist is told to write a note for the supervisor. What should it include?
o: Only the name of the client who was under the dryer
What happened, which dryer, and that it is out of use
A guess about which stylist broke it by using it wrongly
A request for a refund of what the salon paid for the dryer
questions.why: A fault report says what happened, when, which equipment it was and that it was taken out of use. A qualified person decides on repair, and the report helps prevent a repeat.

questions.q: What is the best way to store the new boxes of shampoo that arrive?
o: In front of the old stock, where they are easiest to see
On top of the old stock, so the shelf looks full
Behind the old stock, so the oldest is used first
In the staff area, where the stylists can reach them
questions.why: First in, first out: the oldest stock is used before newer stock so nothing goes out of date. New stock goes behind the old, and expiry dates are checked.

questions.q: Which action will do most to cut the salon's electricity bill?
o: Switching off and unplugging dryers when not in use
Keeping the dryers on a low setting for the whole day
Opening the front door to let hot air out of the salon
Using the washing machine for a single towel at a time
questions.why: Equipment left switched on uses electricity even when nobody is using it. Switch off and unplug it when finished, and wash full loads. A door open with air conditioning on wastes electricity too.

questions.q: What should Roxanne do about the two dripping taps?
o: Put a cloth under each tap so the drip is not heard
Turn each tap on full for a second to flush the drip out
Ignore them, since a few drops of water cost nothing
Report them to be fixed: drips waste water and money
questions.why: A dripping tap wastes a surprising amount of water over a day, and water costs money. Report it so a repair can be arranged; do not try to repair plumbing you are not trained for.

questions.q: How should Roxanne lift one of the heavy 5-litre bottles from the floor?
o: Bend at the waist with straight legs and lift quickly
Bend her knees, keep her back straight, hold it close
Twist to the side as she lifts so the shelf is nearer
Lift it above her head to put it on the top shelf
questions.why: Bend the knees, keep the back straight, hold the load close and lift with the legs. Do not twist. Heavy items go on low shelves; get help or use a trolley if it is too heavy.

questions.q: A trainee is carrying a pair of scissors across the salon. How should she carry them?
o: Points up, so the blades do not touch her clothes
Held loosely behind her back, so that clients cannot see
In her apron pocket with the points showing at the top
Points down, in a case or closed hand, handle first
questions.why: Scissors are carried with the points down and away from people, ideally in a holder or case, and passed handle first. Loose or pocketed sharp points injure the carrier and others.
